Predictive Modeling for Course Demand and Revenue Forecasting on EduPro

A noise-floor analysis of catalogue demand, and what it implies for pricing strategy.

Abstract

Online learning platforms increasingly seek predictive models to decide which courses to launch, how to price them, and which instructors to onboard. This study builds a complete demand- and revenue-forecasting pipeline over the EduPro Online Platform dataset (60 courses, 60 instructors, 3,000 learners, 10,000 transactions across calendar 2025) and evaluates it against explicit statistical baselines.

The principal result is negative, and precisely quantified. Course-level enrollment demand is statistically indistinguishable from uniform random allocation (χ² = 55.52, df = 59, p = 0.60; index of dispersion = 0.941). A variance decomposition shows total cross-course variance (156.8) falls below the sampling variance implied by multinomial allocation (163.9), which places the maximum attainable out-of-sample R² at 0.00. Consistent with that bound, no model in a six-model zoo spanning linear, penalised and ensemble families achieves practically meaningful skill: the best reaches cross-validated R² = 0.051 ± 0.035 and reduces mean absolute error by 0.45 enrollments on a base of 167 — an improvement of 0.3%. On an out-of-time panel split, every model scores negative R².

Course revenue appears highly predictable (R² = 0.991), but an ablation demonstrates this is an artefact: Revenue ≡ CoursePrice × EnrollmentCount holds to floating-point exactness, and removing price features collapses performance to R² = −0.104. We argue that reporting revenue R² without this ablation constitutes a material overstatement of model capability.

Three findings do survive scrutiny and carry direct commercial consequence. First, 38 of 60 courses (63%) are free; they absorb 64.0% of all enrollments and return zero revenue. Second, price elasticity of demand across the observed 0.78–490.90 range is −0.010 with a 95% confidence interval of [−0.035, +0.015] — bounded near zero, meaning demand did not measurably fall as price rose. Third, two of sixty instructors deliver 60.9% of all transactions across 55 of 60 courses, a concentration risk invisible in revenue reporting. We conclude that for this platform the decision-relevant lever is monetisation coverage, not course selection, and we specify the instrumentation required to make demand prediction viable in future.

Keywords   demand forecasting · revenue prediction · noise floor · predictability limits · price elasticity · educational analytics · baseline comparison

1Introduction

1.1 Motivation

For an online learning platform, forward visibility into demand governs three recurring decisions: which new courses to launch, how to price the existing catalogue, and which instructors to onboard and retain. Each is currently made at EduPro from historical intuition rather than quantified forecasts, and each carries capital or opportunity cost when made wrongly.

The stated objective of this project is to move EduPro from reactive reporting to proactive planning by predicting three targets — enrollment count per course, revenue per course, and aggregated revenue per category — from course attributes, instructor attributes and historical transaction behaviour.

1.2 The question behind the question

A demand model is only useful if demand is, in fact, driven by things the platform can observe and control. Before asking "which model predicts enrollments best?", a prior question must be settled: "how much of enrollment variation is explainable at all?"

This distinction matters more than it is usually given credit for. A model reporting R² = 0.05 admits two readings that call for opposite responses:

  1. The model is inadequate — try more features, more capacity, better tuning.
  2. The data contains no signal — no amount of modelling effort will help, and the correct action is to instrument new data sources.

Machine-learning practice defaults to reading (1). This study establishes a noise floor — a variance-decomposition bound on attainable R² — which discriminates between the two readings before any model is fitted. We regard establishing that bound as the primary methodological contribution here.

1.3 Contributions

  1. A complete, reproducible pipeline from raw workbook to deployed dashboard, implementing the full specified methodology (feature engineering, baseline and advanced models, MAE/RMSE/R² evaluation, feature-importance analysis).
  2. A noise-floor diagnostic that bounds attainable predictive performance a priori, with supporting dispersion, independence and multiple-testing-corrected screens.
  3. An ablation protocol that separates genuine predictive skill from recovered accounting identities in revenue models.
  4. A quantified statement of the commercial levers the evidence supports, and an instrumentation roadmap for the ones it does not yet.

2Background

2.1 Demand prediction in course catalogues

Course demand is conventionally modelled as a function of content attributes (topic, level, duration), commercial attributes (price, free/paid), quality signals (ratings) and supply-side attributes (instructor reputation, experience). The implicit causal model is that learners survey a catalogue and select on observable quality-adjusted value.

That model presumes learners see the catalogue in a way the data records. In practice, the dominant determinants of which course a learner enrols in are typically placement, recommendation, search ranking and marketing exposure — none of which appear in transaction-level records. This gap between recorded outcomes and causal drivers is central to the results reported here.

2.2 Baselines and the credibility of forecasting claims

Forecasting literature has long insisted that a model be compared against naive alternatives — the mean, the last observation, a seasonal naive — because complex models routinely fail to beat them on noisy series. We adopt that convention throughout: every comparison table in this paper reports a mean baseline, and the panel tables add last-month-naive and course-history-mean baselines. Skill is reported as proportional RMSE reduction against the baseline, not as raw R².

2.3 Public-sector relevance

The same catalogue-planning problem recurs in public recreation programming. The City of Toronto's Parks, Forestry & Recreation division stewards more than 1,500 parks and 8,000 hectares, and its Community Recreation unit operates a registered-program catalogue across recreation centres, rinks and pools. Its stated priorities include modernising front-line client services and developing a Parks and Recreation Facilities Master Plan — both of which require exactly the forecast this study attempts: which programs will fill, and what they will return. The methodological caution developed below applies with more force in that setting, where a confidently-wrong forecast misallocates public funds.

3Data

3.1 Source

EduPro Online Platform.xlsx, four sheets covering calendar year 2025 (2025-01-01 to 2025-12-30).

3.2 Quality audit

The dataset is unusually clean. All fourteen integrity checks pass: zero missing cells across all sheets, zero orphan foreign keys in any of the three transaction relationships, zero duplicate identifiers, zero negative amounts, zero duplicate (user, course) pairs, and every one of the 60 courses carries transactions.

Cleanliness of this order is itself informative — it is characteristic of synthetically generated records rather than production logs, and it anticipates the distributional findings of Section 5.

3.3 Descriptive structure

QuantityValue
Enrollments per coursemean 166.7, SD 12.5, range 140–196
Total revenue911,323.47
Free courses38 of 60 (63%), 6,403 enrollments, revenue 0
Paid courses22 of 60 (37%), 3,597 enrollments, mean transaction 253.36
Paid price range0.78 – 490.90
Course ratingmean 3.10, SD 1.17
Course durationmean 27.6 h, SD 16.1 h
Instructor ratingmean 3.13, SD 0.95
Instructor experiencemean 6.3 y, range 1–24 y
Categories12, exactly 5 courses each

Two structural features shape the analysis.

The revenue identity. Every transaction Amount equals the CoursePrice of the course exactly (maximum absolute deviation 3.6 × 10⁻¹² over 10,000 rows). There are no discounts, coupons, refunds or partial payments. Consequently CourseRevenue ≡ CoursePrice × EnrollmentCount is an accounting identity, not an empirical relationship.

The instructor–course mapping is many-to-many. Transactions attach a TeacherID, but each course is delivered by a median of 14 distinct teachers and each teacher appears across a median of 15 courses. There is no stable course owner. We therefore define course-level instructor features as unweighted averages over the distinct teachers who delivered the course — deliberately unweighted, because weighting by transaction volume would leak the target variable into the features.

4Methodology

4.1 Analysis tables

Two tables are constructed, addressing different decisions:

  • Course-level (cross-sectional), n = 60. One row per course, attributes only. Supports the launch decision: if we build this, what will it do? A new course has no history, so no historical features may be used.
  • Course-month panel, n = 720 (540 after lag warm-up). One row per course per month, dense (no empty cells). Supports operational planning: what will each course do next month?

4.2 Feature engineering

Course features. Price bands (Free / Low <100 / Medium <300 / High ≥300); duration buckets (Short <10h / Medium <25h / Long <40h / Extended ≥40h); rating tiers (Poor <2 / Fair <3 / Good <4 / Excellent ≥4); ordinal course-level encoding (Beginner 0, Intermediate 1, Advanced 2); price-per-hour; a paid indicator.

Instructor features. Experience buckets (Junior <3y / Mid <7y / Senior <12y / Veteran ≥12y); mean and maximum instructor rating; mean and maximum experience; expertise–category match score, the share of the delivery team whose Expertise equals the CourseCategory (catalogue mean 0.478, against a chance baseline of 0.083 given 12 categories); delivery concentration as a Herfindahl index over the teacher mix; QualitySignal, the product of course rating and mean instructor rating.

Historical performance features (panel only). Enrollment lags at 1, 2 and 3 months; 3-month rolling mean of enrollments and revenue; expanding course mean; revenue lag 1; expanding revenue-per-enrollment; month index.

4.3 Leakage controls

Three specific hazards were identified and closed:

  1. Volume-weighted instructor features would encode the target. Averages are taken over distinct teachers instead.
  2. Contemporaneous history would trivially predict the target. All panel features use groupby(course).shift(k), so row t sees only months strictly before t; rows with an incomplete 3-month window are dropped (720 → 540).
  3. Preprocessing fitted on the full dataset would leak distributional information across folds. Scaling and one-hot encoding are inside the scikit-learn Pipeline and are therefore refit within every fold.

4.4 Models

TierModelConfiguration
BaselineMean predictorDummyRegressor(strategy="mean")
BaselineLinear RegressionOLS
BaselineRidge RegressionRidgeCV, 25 alphas, 10⁻³–10³
BaselineLasso RegressionLassoCV, 25 alphas, nested CV
AdvancedRandom Forest300 trees, min_samples_leaf 2, max_features sqrt
AdvancedGradient Boosting200 stages, lr 0.05, depth 3, subsample 0.9

Preprocessing: StandardScaler on 13 numeric features, OneHotEncoder(drop="first") on 3 categoricals. RANDOM_STATE = 42 throughout.

4.5 Validation

Cross-sectional. With n = 60, a single hold-out split of 12 rows is too unstable to interpret. We therefore use repeated 5-fold CV (5 repeats, different shuffles), pooling out-of-fold predictions within each repeat before scoring, and report the mean and standard deviation of the metric across repeats. Leave-one-out CV is run alongside as a second, lower-bias estimate.

Panel. Strict out-of-time split: train on the earlier months, test on the final three. No shuffling — the test set lies entirely in the future of the training set.

Metrics. MAE (average error magnitude), RMSE (penalises large errors), R² (variance explained). We add skill, the proportional RMSE reduction against the mean baseline, because R² alone obscures how small an absolute improvement can be.

4.6 The noise floor

For a catalogue of K courses receiving N total enrollments, the null hypothesis that all courses are equally attractive implies multinomial allocation with per-course variance

σ²sampling = N · (1/K) · (1 − 1/K)

Observed cross-course variance decomposes as σ²total = σ²systematic + σ²sampling. Since only the systematic component is in principle explainable by covariates, the maximum attainable out-of-sample R² is

R²max = σ²systematic / σ²total = 1 − σ²sampling / σ²total

This bound is computed before any model is fitted, and every model score is reported against it.

5Predictability diagnostics

5.1 Demand is indistinguishable from random allocation

With N = 10,000 and K = 60, the null predicts 166.7 enrollments per course with a standard deviation of 12.80. Observed: mean 166.7, standard deviation 12.52 — no larger than chance.

TestStatisticpReading
Uniform-allocation χ²55.52 (df 59)0.60Cannot reject equal demand
Index of dispersion0.941—1.00 = pure Poisson noise
Course × month independenceχ² = 612.9 (df 649)0.84No course-specific seasonality
Monthly trend (OLS slope)+0.97 /month0.79No trend
Monthly total dispersionχ² = 21.11 (df 11)0.032Mild platform-level over-dispersion
The noise floor

σ²total = 156.8, σ²sampling = 163.9. Total variance is below sampling variance, giving σ²systematic = 0 and R²max = 0.00.

The only test returning nominal significance is platform-wide monthly dispersion (p = 0.032): aggregate volume varies by ±40 enrollments per month against a Poisson expectation of ±29. With twelve observations this is marginal, and it concerns platform totals rather than any course-level driver.

5.2 Feature screen with multiple-testing correction

Fifteen candidate drivers were screened univariately (Spearman for numeric, ANOVA for categorical) with Bonferroni correction.

On the one survivor. QualitySignal — the product of course rating and mean instructor rating — survives correction at ρ = 0.381, adjusted p = 0.040. We report this rather than suppress it, and we judge it a selection artefact for three reasons. First, it is the largest of fifteen screened correlations, and Bonferroni bounds the family-wise error rate rather than eliminating it. Second, the omnibus dispersion test is decisive in the opposite direction: if a genuine driver existed, cross-course spread would exceed the random null, and it does not — it is slightly narrower. Third, and conclusively, out-of-sample validation is the arbiter: a real driver improves held-out prediction. Section 6.1 shows it does not.

This is the reason the noise floor is computed first. Without it, ρ = 0.38 with p = 0.003 reads as a finding.

5.3 Price elasticity

A constant-elasticity specification log(enrollments) = a + b·log(price) over the 22 paid courses gives:

b = −0.0096    95% CI [−0.0346, +0.0155]    p = 0.44    R² = 0.031

The interval is the substantive result. Elasticity is not merely "not significant" — it is bounded within ±0.035 across a price range spanning 0.78 to 490.90. A 10% price increase is estimated to cost between 0.35% and −0.16% of demand. Over this catalogue and this range, demand did not respond to price.

Two caveats are essential. Prices were not randomly assigned, so this is an observational estimate vulnerable to confounding; and the finding is inseparable from Section 5.1 — demand did not respond to price because it did not respond to anything. The appropriate response is a randomised pricing experiment, not a catalogue-wide reprice.

Gradient Boosting11.3313.73−0.223 ± 0.067−0.032−9.0%

Three observations.

Nothing clears the noise floor meaningfully. The best model reaches R² = 0.051 against a bound of 0.00 — within 1.5 standard deviations of zero across repeats, and consistent with the sampling error of the R² estimate itself on 60 rows.

The improvement is economically void. Random Forest reduces MAE from 10.17 to 9.72: 0.45 enrollments on a mean of 166.7, or 0.3%. No launch, pricing or staffing decision changes on that margin.

Unregularised Linear Regression is actively harmful (R² = −0.466). With 13 numeric features, 3 one-hot-expanded categoricals and 60 rows, OLS overfits severely. That Ridge and Lasso recover to ≈0 is a textbook demonstration that regularisation is doing exactly what it should — shrinking toward the mean, which is the correct answer.

The QualitySignal question from Section 5.2 resolves here: models with access to it do not beat the mean baseline out of sample. Its in-sample correlation does not generalise.

6.2 Course revenue, and the ablation

Feature setBest modelCV MAECV RMSECV R²Skill
All features (price included)Lasso1,4662,4060.991+90.6%
Price features removedRidge20,86826,446−0.104−3.2%

Taken alone, the first row is an excellent result — R² = 0.991 on out-of-fold predictions, with linear models beating Random Forest (0.889) because the underlying relationship is exactly linear in price.

That is the tell. Since Revenue ≡ Price × Enrollments holds exactly and enrollments are near-constant at 166.7, revenue is essentially 166.7 × Price. The model recovers a multiplication.

Why the ablation matters

Removing CoursePrice, PricePerHour, PriceBandOrd and CourseType drops every model below zero; the best is Ridge at −0.104, worse than predicting the mean. All apparent revenue predictability comes from price, none from demand behaviour.

We would argue this ablation should be mandatory wherever a target is an arithmetic function of an available feature. Without it, this project could have reported "R² = 0.99 revenue forecasting" as a headline. It would have been true and substantively worthless.

For the ten categories earning above 1,000, mean APE is 5.8% and median 5.4%. Portfolio total is accurate to +1.7% (911,323 actual vs 926,655 predicted).

Two honest caveats. Machine Learning's 1188% error reflects a 133-unit denominator (four of its five courses are free, the fifth priced at 0.78), not a model failure — but it does show percentage error is meaningless at near-zero revenue. More seriously, the unconstrained linear model predicts negative revenue for Marketing. Revenue is non-negative by construction; a floor at zero, or a log-link / Tweedie GLM, is required before operational use. This is a genuine defect in the current artefact.

Every standard deviation exceeds its mean, most by several-fold. No feature has an importance distinguishable from zero across folds. The ranking is noise ordering itself.

Standardised Ridge coefficients give in-sample direction: QualitySignal +1.35, PriceBandOrd −1.18, Data Science category +1.07, InstructorAvgExperience +1.04, CourseRating +0.88 enrollments per standard deviation. The largest effect in the catalogue is 1.35 enrollments per SD — 0.8% of mean course demand. Even taking these at face value and ignoring their statistical fragility, they are too small to inform any decision.

For revenue, permutation importance is dominated by CoursePrice (1.56 × 10⁸), PriceBandOrd (9.39 × 10⁷) and PricePerHour (8.76 × 10⁷) — three encodings of the same quantity, two orders of magnitude above CourseRating (2.27 × 10⁶). The identity again.

7Business findings

7.1 The monetisation gap

Demand is uniform across categories (enrollment shares span 8.1%–9.2%). Revenue is not: the top three categories take 60.7% of it. Since demand is flat, that divergence is caused by pricing coverage alone.

The core commercial finding

Marketing attracts 806 enrollments — statistically identical to AI's 829 — and returns nothing, because all five of its courses are free. AI returns 202,751 from the same demand because four of its five courses are priced. Platform-wide, 6,403 of 10,000 enrollments (64.0%) are monetised at zero.

7.2 What conversion is worth

Courses convertedAt 25At 49At 99
10 (of 38)+25,000+49,000+99,000
19 (half)+47,500+93,100+188,100
38 (all)+95,000+186,200+376,200
 Assumes 40% of a converted course's demand is lost on introducing a charge — deliberately pessimistic, since the measured elasticity implies far less.

Against a base of 911,323, converting half the free catalogue at 49 yields +10.2% annual revenue; all of it at 99 yields +41%.

These are scenario arithmetic, not forecasts. Their value is in ordering the options: even under pessimistic churn, pricing coverage dominates any plausible gain from better course selection — which the modelling shows is worth 0.3%.

7.3 Instructor concentration

Two instructors of sixty — TC00040 (Cybersecurity, 24 years, rating 4.58) and TC00042 (Machine Learning, 21 years, rating 4.97) — account for 60.9% of all 10,000 transactions, each appearing across 55 of the 60 courses. The remaining 58 instructors handle a median of 56 transactions each.

This is uncorrelated with demand (r = 0.002, p = 0.99), so it is not a driver to model. It is an operational exposure: the departure of either individual affects the majority of delivery. It does not appear in any revenue report, which is precisely why it is worth surfacing.

Separately, expertise–category alignment runs at 47.8% against a chance baseline of 8.3% — assignment is far from random — but alignment shows no relationship with enrollment (ρ = 0.080, p = 0.55).

8Recommendations

  1. Do not deploy the enrollment model as a ranking tool. It cannot distinguish a good course from a bad one; the evidence is that within this catalogue there is no such distinction to detect. It is fit for capacity sizing — every course draws approximately 167 enrollments per year — and the dashboard states this on the prediction screen rather than burying it.
  2. Run a randomised pricing experiment. The elasticity estimate is bounded near zero but observational. Randomly assign price changes across a matched subset for one quarter. This is the single highest-value data-collection action available.
  3. Convert free courses in a staged pilot. Begin with 8–10 free courses in categories with proven willingness to pay (Data Science, Programming, Cybersecurity all have paid courses selling at 200+). Price at 25–49. Measure demand loss directly rather than assuming it.
  4. Forecast at the platform level. Aggregate monthly volume is stable at 833 ± 40 and forecastable; per-course monthly demand is not. Set planning cadence accordingly.
  5. Address instructor concentration. Establish delivery coverage as a tracked operational metric and reduce single-person exposure across the catalogue.
  6. Instrument the demand drivers. The dataset records outcomes but not causes.

9Limitations

Sample size. 60 courses is small for cross-sectional modelling. Repeated K-fold and LOOCV mitigate but do not eliminate the resulting instability; the ±0.035 standard deviation on the best R² reflects it honestly.

Single year, no price variation within courses. Twelve months cannot separate seasonality from noise, and no course changed price, so elasticity is identified only across courses — vulnerable to confounding by category, quality and positioning.

Synthetic data characteristics. Zero missing values, exact price–amount correspondence, uniform 5-courses-per-category structure and multinomial-consistent demand together indicate generated rather than observed records. The negative findings are therefore properly read as a finding about this dataset, not about online course demand in general. The methodology — noise floor first, ablation always, baselines throughout — transfers regardless.

Instructor attribution. The many-to-many transaction–teacher mapping means "the instructor of a course" is not well defined. Unweighted distinct-teacher averages avoid target leakage but blur genuine instructor effects if any existed.

Non-negativity. The deployed revenue model is unconstrained and can predict negative revenue (Section 6.4). A zero floor or a log-link GLM is required before operational use. This is stated as an outstanding defect, not a resolved one.

Observational throughout. No causal claim is made. Every recommendation involving a change to price or catalogue is framed as an experiment to run.

10Conclusion

This study set out to build predictive models for course enrollment and revenue on the EduPro platform. The models were built, evaluated properly, and — for enrollment demand — do not work. The contribution is establishing why, with enough precision to act on.

Course-level demand in this dataset is statistically indistinguishable from uniform random allocation (p = 0.60, dispersion 0.941), and a variance decomposition places the maximum attainable R² at zero. Six models across three families converge on that bound, on both a cross-sectional and an out-of-time panel design. Revenue's apparent R² of 0.991 is an accounting identity, demonstrated by an ablation that collapses it to −0.104.

A negative result stated with a bound is not a failed project. Reporting R² = 0.05 as "the model needs more tuning" would have sent EduPro after a signal that provably is not there. Reporting it as "the maximum attainable R² is 0.00, and here is the instrumentation needed to change that" redirects the same effort somewhere it can pay.

Meanwhile the data does support a specific, quantified commercial finding: 64% of enrollments are monetised at zero, measured price elasticity is bounded within ±0.035, and converting half the free catalogue at a modest price is worth roughly 10% of annual revenue even under pessimistic churn — two orders of magnitude more than perfect course selection could deliver.

The most valuable thing a predictive model produced here was a reliable statement about what cannot yet be predicted.

AReproducibility

Every number in this paper regenerates from the raw workbook in roughly three minutes, with RANDOM_STATE = 42 throughout:

pip install -r requirements.txt
python -m src.run_pipeline
python -m src.figures
streamlit run app.py

Result tables are written to reports/tables/ (data-quality audit, feature screen, monetisation gap, predictability diagnostics, cross-sectional and panel model comparisons, importance tables, Ridge coefficients, category revenue). Figures render to reports/figures/. The full console transcript is committed at reports/pipeline_log.txt.
